0.title: Good Gifts in a Fallen World
0.essay:
The man next door has never been to church, yet he would give you the coat off his back. The surgeon who mended your daughter’s heart does not believe in God. The music that moved you to tears last week was written by a man who mocked the faith. If the Bible is right that all people are sinners, how can this be?

A real puzzle

Christians believe that sin has spoiled every part of us. The Bible says “None is righteous, no, not one” (Romans 3:10). And yet unbelievers love their children, cure diseases, build bridges that do not fall down, run honest businesses and fair courts, and make things of great beauty. Jesus himself took this for granted: “If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:11). How does that happen?

The answer: God is good to all

The answer is not that people are better than the Bible says. It is that God is kinder than we imagined. “The LORD is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made” (Psalm 145:9). Every day he holds back the full force of human evil, and every day he pours out gifts on people who never thank him. Christians call this common grace: “common” because everyone shares it, “grace” because no one deserves it.

The study The Grace of God touches on common grace briefly; this study takes it slowly. Its aim is simple: that you would look at a harvest field, a hospital or a symphony and see the kindness of God, and be led by it to his Son.

The chapters

The Goodness God Shows to All; Sin Held Back; Gifts Through Every Hand; Patience That Leads Somewhere; Where Christians Differ; and Living by Common Grace.

For reflection

Think of someone you know who does not share your faith but is kind, honest or gifted. How have you explained that to yourself until now? What might change if you saw their goodness as a gift from God?

1.title: The Goodness God Shows to All
1.essay:
Every sunrise is a sermon. Every harvest is a letter from God. Long before anyone hears the gospel, they are surrounded by his kindness: food on the table, breath in their lungs, the laughter of a child. The Bible calls us to notice this, and to ask who is giving it.

What common grace is

Common grace is God’s undeserved kindness to all people, believers and unbelievers alike. It has two sides. God holds back sin, so that the world is not as bad as it could be. And God gives good gifts, so that life in a fallen world is still full of good things. It is called grace because none of it is earned. A rebel against the King has no right to the King’s bread, and yet he eats it every day.

It begins with a promise

After the flood, God made a solemn promise. He knew exactly what he was dealing with: “the intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth.” And yet he said, “While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease” (Genesis 8:21–22). Then he made a covenant “with every living creature” (Genesis 9:10), and set the rainbow in the cloud as its sign (Genesis 9:13).

Notice what this covenant does and does not do. It does not forgive sins or promise eternal life. It promises that the world will go on. Seasons will turn, crops will grow, families will multiply, and human life will be protected by justice (Genesis 9:6). The study Covenant Theology explains that this covenant is about preservation, not salvation. God keeps the stage standing so that the drama of redemption can be played out on it. Every rainbow since is a reminder that God is holding back the waters.

A kindness Jesus pointed to

The psalmist sees it everywhere: “The eyes of all look to you, and you give them their food in due season. You open your hand; you satisfy the desire of every living thing” (Psalm 145:15–16). Not the desire of every believer. Every living thing.

Jesus builds a whole command on it. “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:44–45). In Luke he is even plainer: the Father “is kind to the ungrateful and the evil” (Luke 6:35). This is not reluctant tolerance. Jesus calls it kindness, and tells us to copy it.

A witness to the nations

Paul preached the same truth to people who had never opened a Bible. In Lystra he told a crowd of pagans that God “did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness” (Acts 14:17). Every meal they had eaten was a message from the God they did not know.

In Athens he went further. God “himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything” (Acts 17:25). He decided where and when the nations would live, “that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us” (Acts 17:27). The air every philosopher breathed was on loan from God. Common grace is not a distant God tossing scraps. It is a near God, holding every life in his hand.

Not saving grace

Here we must be careful. Common grace is real grace, but it is not saving grace. It does not forgive sin, give a new heart or bring anyone to heaven. A person can enjoy a lifetime of rain and harvest, health and love, and still be lost. Saving grace is God’s free favour to sinners in Christ, by which he makes the dead alive, forgives them and keeps them for ever; the study The Grace of God sets it out in its chapter Saving Grace.

Think of two gifts from the same father. One is the food he puts on the table for everyone in the house, including the lodger who despises him. The other is adoption: his name, his inheritance, his heart. Common grace is the first. Saving grace is the second. Both are kind. Only one makes you a child.

Yet the two are not strangers. The same God gives both, and the first points to the second. The God who feeds his enemies is the God who sent his Son to die for them. Every loaf of bread whispers what the cross says aloud: God is kinder than we deserve.

An example

A young woman had always assumed that her non-Christian parents’ love for her was simply “natural”, and that God had nothing to do with it. Reading Psalm 145 one evening, she stops at the words “The LORD is good to all” (Psalm 145:9). She realises that every packed lunch, every lift to the station, every word of comfort from her father was a gift that came through his hands from God’s. She begins to thank God for her parents, and to pray, with fresh warmth, that they would meet the Giver.

For reflection

What did God promise Noah after the flood, and why does that promise matter to you today? Why does Jesus point to the sun and the rain when he tells us to love our enemies? What is the difference between common grace and saving grace? Where have you received God’s kindness this week without noticing it?

2.title: Sin Held Back
2.essay:
Imagine a river held back by a great dam. On a calm day you might forget the dam is there. But if it were removed, the valley below would be swept away. Human sin is like that river, and God, in his kindness, has built many dams.

Not as bad as it could be

The Bible’s verdict on the human heart is severe. Before the flood, “every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (Genesis 6:5). “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick” (Jeremiah 17:9). Reformed Christians call this total depravity. But total depravity does not mean that every person is as wicked as they could possibly be. It means that sin has reached every part of us, so that no part is left untouched and no one, by nature, loves God as they should. The study The Truth About Sin explains this in its chapter Where Sin Came From and How Far It Reaches.

So why is the world not worse? Not because the river is shallow, but because God holds it back. Scripture shows several of the ways he does it.

Conscience

God has written something of his law on every human heart. Paul says that when Gentiles who never had the law “by nature do what the law requires,” they “show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them” (Romans 2:14–15). That inner voice which makes a thief uneasy, or a liar blush, is God’s doing. It is damaged and can be silenced, but it is there. Almost every culture on earth has known that murder, betrayal and cruelty to children are wrong. That is not an accident.

Government

After the flood God gave a command that founded human justice: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image” (Genesis 9:6). Paul later says that the ruler “is God’s servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain” (Romans 13:4). Police, courts and laws are often imperfect, and sometimes wicked. But even a poor government usually restrains more evil than it causes. A fair court, run by people who may not know God, is still God’s gift. The study The Christian & the World discusses government more fully in its chapter God and Government.

Family and shame

God restrains sin through the family. A father’s steady discipline, a mother’s watchful eye and the hope of a grandparent’s approval keep countless young people from folly. He also uses the ordinary pressure of what others think. Many people do not cheat simply because they would be ashamed to be found out. That is not holiness, but a wise God puts even our unworthy motives to work for the protection of others.

God’s own hand

Sometimes God holds back sin directly. When the pagan king Abimelech took Abraham’s wife into his household, not knowing she was married, God told him in a dream, “it was I who kept you from sinning against me. Therefore I did not let you touch her” (Genesis 20:6). How many sins have you been kept from in ways you will never know? A delayed train, an interrupted conversation, a sudden check in the mind: God is at work in all of it.

Paul speaks of a restraint on evil in the whole of history. Of the coming man of lawlessness he writes, “you know what is restraining him now … Only he who now restrains it will do so until he is out of the way” (2 Thessalonians 2:6–7). Christians have understood this restrainer in different ways. This commentary takes it most likely to be God’s providence working through government and law. Either way, the point is clear: evil is on a leash, and God holds it.

When God lets go

Romans 1 shows what happens when the restraint is loosened. Three times Paul says “God gave them up” (Romans 1:24; see also 1:26, 28). This is a terrible judgment: God steps back and lets people have what they want. That should make us grateful for every day the dam holds, and keep us praying for our nations.

What this means for us

This truth humbles us. If you have not committed some great crime, it may be partly because of a godly upbringing, a fear of disgrace or circumstances you did not choose. “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). It also frees us from naivety: the kindness of an unbeliever is real, but it is not proof that the heart is fine without Christ.

And it points us to the cross. The God who restrains sin in the world is the God who dealt with sin itself at Calvary. Restraint holds the river back. Only Christ can dry up its source and give a new heart.

An example

A man in his fifties, converted late in life, looks back on his twenties with a shudder. He was angry and reckless, and more than once came close to doing something that would have ruined lives. What stopped him? A grandmother’s face he could not bear to disappoint, a friend who took the car keys, a sleepless night of conscience. Then he realises: God was holding him back long before he knew God’s name.

For reflection

What does total depravity mean, and what does it not mean? Which of the ways God restrains sin (conscience, government, family, shame, his own hand) have you seen at work in your own life? Why should Christians be grateful for government, even imperfect government? How does knowing that you have been held back from sin make you more humble?

3.title: Gifts Through Every Hand
3.essay:
The first musicians in the Bible came from the family of a murderer. The temple of God was built with the help of foreign craftsmen. A pagan emperor is called the Lord’s anointed. Scripture is not embarrassed by the gifts of unbelievers. It traces every one of them back to God.

From Cain’s line

Genesis 4 tells of Cain, who killed his brother and went out from the presence of the LORD. Within a few generations his family produced remarkable things. Jabal “was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock.” Jubal “was the father of all those who play the lyre and pipe.” Tubal-cain “was the forger of all instruments of bronze and iron” (Genesis 4:20–22). Farming, music and metalwork, the beginnings of culture, came through a family that had turned from God.

Their rebellion was not good. But God did not withdraw his gifts. Outside Eden, human beings still bear his image, and he still pours out skill and invention on them.

Skill is God’s gift

When the tabernacle was built, God said of Bezalel, “I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship, to devise artistic designs” (Exodus 31:3–4). He adds, “I have given to all able men ability” (Exodus 31:6). Bezalel was a believer, and his gift was special. But the principle reaches wider. Isaiah says even a farmer’s know-how comes from God: “his God teaches him … This also comes from the LORD of hosts; he is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom” (Isaiah 28:26, 29).

When Solomon built the temple, he hired the servants of Hiram king of Tyre, because, as he admitted, “there is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians” (1 Kings 5:6). A craftsman from Tyre, also called Hiram, “was full of wisdom, understanding, and skill for making any work in bronze” (1 Kings 7:14). The house of God was built partly by hands from a pagan city, and the Bible records it without a blush.

Rulers God uses

Most striking of all, God calls the Persian king Cyrus “his anointed” and says, “I call you by your name … though you do not know me” (Isaiah 45:1, 4). Cyrus let the exiles go home to rebuild Jerusalem. He did not worship Israel’s God, but God gave him power and used it for good. Good leadership is one of the great gifts of common grace; the study Leadership explores it.

Truth wherever it is found

Paul could quote pagan poets. In Athens he said, “as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are indeed his offspring’” (Acts 17:28), a line from the Greek poet Aratus. To Titus he quoted a Cretan writer, traditionally thought to be Epimenides, and added, “This testimony is true” (Titus 1:13). Paul did not think their religion was true. But he recognised that what they had said, in that sentence, was true.

Augustine taught that a good Christian should understand that wherever he finds truth, it belongs to his Lord. This is often summed up as “all truth is God’s truth.” John Calvin made the same point strongly. He argued that since the Spirit of God is the only fountain of truth, we must never reject or despise truth wherever it appears, unless we want to dishonour the Spirit himself. He admired the ancient lawyers, philosophers, doctors and mathematicians, and called their gifts excellent gifts of the Spirit, given even to the ungodly for the good of the human race.

A world full of gifts

Look around. Rain and harvest. The beauty of a mountain range and a well-made chair. Marriage and the joy of children, which God gives in every nation. Medicine, from the first herbal remedy to modern surgery. Science, which studies an orderly world that God made and holds together (Colossians 1:17); the study Faith & Science explores this. Technology, from the plough to the phone, with its blessings and its dangers; see the study Technology & the Christian Mind. Law and order, schools, and the stories and songs that make us laugh and weep.

“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17). The gift may pass through a believer’s hands or an unbeliever’s. Its source is the same. “The earth is full of the steadfast love of the LORD” (Psalm 33:5).

Gifts, not the Giver

None of this means that every product of human culture is good. The skill that makes a scalpel can make a weapon. Gifts are bent by the sinful hearts that use them. So Christians receive them with thanks and with discernment: “test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

But the main lesson is wonder. Behind every gifted surgeon, every skilful builder and every haunting melody is the generosity of God. And behind all of these stands the greatest gift of all. The Word through whom all things were made, “the true light, which gives light to everyone” (John 1:9), came into the world to give not only skill and beauty, but himself.

An example

A church musician used to feel guilty for loving the music of a composer whose life was far from Christ. She wondered whether she should give it up. Reading Genesis 4 and Exodus 31, she realises that the gift of music came from God before it came through any composer. Now, when she listens, she still notices what is wrong in the composer’s world, but she also thanks God for the beauty he gave through him.

For reflection

What does Genesis 4 teach about where human culture came from? Why do you think the Bible is so open about unbelievers helping to build the temple? What does it mean that “all truth is God’s truth”? Which good gift, given through someone who does not know God, are you most grateful for today?

4.title: Patience That Leads Somewhere
4.essay:
God’s kindness to the world is not aimless. It is not the absent-minded generosity of a rich man who has stopped paying attention. It has a purpose. Every gift, every day of delay, is a hand stretched out, calling people home.

Kindness with a purpose

Paul asks a searching question: “do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4). The goodness of God is not meant to make us comfortable in sin. It is meant to make us ask, “Who is this God who keeps being kind to me? And how have I treated him?”

Peter says the same about the delay of judgment. People mock that Christ has not returned. But “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). Every day the world goes on is a day of mercy. God is not idle. He is waiting, and his waiting is an invitation.

Judgment held back for a time

In Athens, Paul told his hearers that God had “overlooked” the times of ignorance, “but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:30–31). Common grace is like a stay of execution. The sentence is real, but it has not yet been carried out. That is why the same God who sends rain on the unjust will one day judge them.

So common grace does not last for ever. It belongs to this age, the time between the flood and the final day. Then God’s kindness to those who have refused him will end, and only those who have taken refuge in Christ will go on into the new creation.

It can be resisted

Here is the sad side. Common grace can be resisted, and very often is. Paul says that all people know something of God from the world he has made: “his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse.” And yet, “although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him” (Romans 1:20–21). People “suppress the truth” (Romans 1:18).

Isaiah saw it too: “If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness” (Isaiah 26:10). Kindness alone does not change a heart. A person can receive a lifetime of gifts and never once look up. That is why common grace leaves people without excuse rather than without need. It shows them enough to make them responsible, but not enough to save them. Only the gospel, applied by the Spirit, can do that.

Gifts and the Giver

The great danger is to love the gifts and ignore the Giver. Picture a child who receives birthday presents every year from a father he never speaks to. He enjoys the presents. He boasts about them. He even thinks he earned them. But he never comes home. The presents were meant to bring him to his father, and he has made them a substitute for him.

That is what idolatry is: taking God’s good gifts, such as sex, money, beauty, achievement or family, and treating them as if they were God. The study What Is Man? shows how our hearts turn good things into ultimate things. Common grace is a signpost, and it is foolish to set up home at the foot of a signpost.

Preparing the way

Yet God often uses common grace to prepare the way for saving grace. Think how many people first met the love of Christ through a kind act: a doctor who took time to listen, a neighbour who brought soup, a teacher who would not give up on them. A good law that protects freedom of worship lets the gospel be preached. Peaceful streets let churches meet. Literacy lets people read the Bible. Medicine keeps people alive long enough to hear. None of these saves anyone. But God weaves them into his saving purposes.

Wonder at his patience

Stop and consider how patient God is. Every day billions of people breathe his air, eat his food and use his gifts, and most never thank him. He could end it in a moment. Instead he keeps giving, and keeps calling. “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live” (Ezekiel 33:11).

This patience has a face. It is seen most clearly in Jesus, who wept over Jerusalem, ate with sinners and prayed for those who crucified him. The patience of God in common grace is the patience that sent his Son.

An example

A woman spent years enjoying a comfortable life: good health, a happy marriage, a successful career. She felt no need of God. Then her husband fell seriously ill, and a Christian nurse cared for him with unusual kindness. Sitting by the bed one night, the woman begins to wonder for the first time where all her good years had come from, and who she should have thanked. She starts reading the Gospels, and the gifts she took for granted become the road home.

For reflection

According to Romans 2:4, what is God’s kindness meant to do? Why does common grace leave people “without excuse” rather than saved? In what ways do you tend to love God’s gifts more than God himself? Can you think of a time when an ordinary kindness prepared the way for someone to hear the gospel?

5.title: Where Christians Differ
5.essay:
Common grace is widely held among Reformed Christians, but it has not been held without debate. Some have built great things on it; others have denied it altogether. The disagreement is worth understanding, because each side is trying to protect something precious.

Calvin

John Calvin (1509–1564) did not build a full doctrine under the name “common grace”, but he laid its foundations. In his Institutes he spoke of a general grace of God, and insisted that the gifts of ancient lawyers, philosophers, doctors and artists were real gifts of the Spirit. He also taught that God restrains the wickedness of fallen people, so that even an unbeliever may live an outwardly upright life. But he insisted that none of this can win God’s favour or bring anyone to salvation.

Kuyper and Bavinck

In the Netherlands, Abraham Kuyper (1837–1920), pastor, journalist, founder of the Free University of Amsterdam and later prime minister, made common grace a major theme. His three-volume work Common Grace (published 1902–1904) argued that God’s common grace preserves the world and allows human culture, science and art to develop. Christians should therefore take part in every area of life, because Christ is Lord of it all. Kuyper also stressed the antithesis, the deep difference between belief and unbelief in every field of thought.

His colleague Herman Bavinck (1854–1921) gave an address on common grace in 1894 and wove the theme through his Reformed Dogmatics. Bavinck stressed that grace does not destroy nature but restores it: God’s saving work in Christ does not throw away the created world, but redeems it.

The 1924 three points

In North America the question came to a head in the Christian Reformed Church. In 1924 its Synod, meeting in Kalamazoo, Michigan, adopted what became known as the “three points”. First, that there is a favourable attitude of God toward humanity in general, and not only toward the elect, shown among other ways in the general offer of the gospel. Second, that God restrains sin in the life of individuals and of society. Third, that unregenerate people, though unable to do any saving good, can perform civil good.

Hoeksema and the Protestant Reformed Churches

Herman Hoeksema (1886–1965), a gifted minister in Grand Rapids, opposed these points, together with Henry Danhof and George Ophoff. In 1924 and 1925 they were deposed from their ministries in the Christian Reformed Church, and the congregations that followed them became the Protestant Reformed Churches in America.

Their concerns should be stated fairly. They hold that God’s grace is always particular: he loves and favours his elect, and only them. Rain and sunshine are good gifts from God, but to those who reject him they are not tokens of favour. They deny that God sincerely desires the salvation of those he has not chosen, while still insisting that the gospel be preached to all and that all be called to repent. They hold that the unregenerate do no true good, since nothing done without faith pleases God, and that God controls sin by his providence rather than by a grace that improves the sinner. They are often called hyper-Calvinists by critics, a label they reject. Their deepest concern is to guard the sovereignty and particularity of saving grace, and to keep the church from blending into the world.

Van Til’s qualifications

Cornelius Van Til (1895–1987), who taught apologetics at Westminster Theological Seminary, accepted common grace but sharpened it in his book Common Grace (1947). He warned against using it to claim a “neutral” zone where believers and unbelievers think alike. Unbelievers know true things, he argued, because they live in God’s world and bear his image, but they know them in spite of their unbelief, not because of it. He called common grace “earlier grace”, and expected the contrast between belief and unbelief to grow sharper as history moves toward its end. The study Apologetics introduces his approach.

What is at stake

Both sides want to honour God: one his kindness and sincere call to all, the other the distinctness of his saving love for his people. Both fear real dangers: on one side, a harsh view of God and a church that withdraws from the world; on the other, a blurring of belief and unbelief and a church that loses its saltiness.

This commentary’s view: God shows real, undeserved kindness to all people, believers and unbelievers. Jesus calls it kindness: the Father “is kind to the ungrateful and the evil” (Luke 6:35). God restrains sin through conscience, family and government, and unbelievers can do genuine civil good, though nothing that earns salvation. The gospel is offered freely and sincerely to everyone, and God truly calls all who hear, yet his saving purpose for his elect never fails. Common grace is not saving grace and must never be confused with it. With Van Til we deny any neutral ground: every gift is received either with thanks to God or with ingratitude. And this commentary expects no golden age in which common grace gradually makes the world Christian. The restraint on evil may loosen toward the end (2 Thessalonians 2:6–7), and the world will be made new only at Christ’s return. Until then, Christians gratefully receive and use the good gifts of common grace with discernment.

Holding the debate in love

This is a debate among brothers and sisters who love the doctrines of grace, and those who affirm common grace can learn from the warnings of those who do not. The aim is not to win an argument, but to see God as he is: holy toward sin, sovereign in salvation, and kind beyond our deserving.

An example

A young man raised in a church that denies common grace moves to a city and joins a church that teaches it. At first he fears his new friends are soft on the world. Over coffee with an older elder, he finds they agree on far more than he expected: the sovereignty of God, the depravity of man, the need for new birth. They still differ, but he leaves with respect for both traditions, and a desire to see God’s kindness everywhere without forgetting his holiness.

For reflection

What were the three points adopted in 1924? What concerns led Herman Hoeksema and others to reject them? Why did Van Til warn against using common grace to claim neutral ground? How can you disagree about this with a fellow believer while still honouring them?

6.title: Living by Common Grace
6.essay:
Common grace is not only a doctrine to understand. It changes how we see our neighbours, our work, our culture and our God. A Christian who grasps it walks through the world with open eyes and a thankful heart.

Gratitude for everything good

The first fruit of common grace is thanksgiving. Every good meal, every kind word, every working boiler, every successful operation is a gift from God. “For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:4). This includes good people. Thank God for the honest mechanic, the patient teacher, the fair-minded judge, the kind neighbour, whether or not they know him. Their goodness is real, and it is his gift.

Humility, not superiority

Common grace humbles believers. Christians are not better people by nature. We are sinners saved by grace. If your neighbour is kinder than you, that should not surprise you, and it should not threaten you. It should drive you to your knees. Paul asks, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). The difference between you and an unbeliever is not that you were better, but that God was merciful to you in Christ.

Learning and working together

Because all truth is God’s truth, Christians can learn from unbelievers. A Christian doctor can learn from a non-Christian researcher. A Christian business owner can learn from a skilful competitor. Jesus even said that “the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light” (Luke 16:8). We can work alongside unbelievers in medicine, science, business, politics and the arts, and be glad to do so.

But working together does not mean compromising. We will not lie for a colleague, cheat for a client or celebrate what God calls sin. We cooperate wherever we can, and stand apart wherever we must, always with respect and gentleness.

Receiving culture with discernment

The books, films, music and art of our world come to us as mixed gifts: real beauty and truth, bent by sin. We should neither swallow everything nor reject everything. Paul’s rule is a good one: “whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things” (Philippians 4:8). Ask of any piece of culture: what here is true and beautiful, for which I can thank God? And what here is false or harmful, which I must refuse?

Seeking the good of the city

When the Jews were exiled to Babylon, a pagan city, God told them, “seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare” (Jeremiah 29:7). Christians are called to serve the common good: to be good neighbours, honest workers and faithful citizens. We support good schools, fair laws and care for the poor, as an overflow of God’s kindness to us.

Paul also urges prayer “for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way” (1 Timothy 2:2). Pray for your leaders by name, whether you voted for them or not. Good government is a gift of common grace, and the study Leadership shows how leaders of every kind can serve it.

Every gift a signpost

Above all, see every gift as a signpost. The beauty of a sunset points to the beauty of the One who made it. The kindness of a stranger points to the kindness of God. The healing of a body points to the Healer who will one day raise the dead. The justice of a good court points to the Judge who will set all things right.

And every signpost points finally to Christ. Common grace keeps the world going. Saving grace, found in him alone, makes it new. The God who gives rain to the unjust gave his Son for the ungodly. If you have enjoyed his common gifts all your life without coming to him, then his kindness is calling you now. Turn to the Giver, and receive the gift that lasts for ever.

Every good gift gathered up

The Bible ends with a glorious picture. In the new Jerusalem, “the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it … They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations” (Revelation 21:24, 26). This commentary holds that this creation will be renewed, not discarded. Whatever was truly good in human life, purified of sin, will find its place in God’s new world. “But nothing unclean will ever enter it” (Revelation 21:27). Only those who belong to the Lamb will be there. But they will find that nothing good God ever gave was wasted.

An example

A Christian engineer works on a team where she is the only believer. For years she felt like an outsider. Then she began to see her colleagues’ skill, humour and integrity as gifts from God. She started thanking God for them by name, and praying for them. Her attitude softened, and her friendships grew. When one colleague asked why she always seemed so grateful, she found herself explaining, simply and gladly, about the God who gives every good gift, and the Son he gave for us.

For reflection

Whose goodness, outside the church, will you thank God for this week? How does common grace make you more humble toward unbelievers? What is one way you could seek the welfare of your town or city? Which good gift in your life could become a signpost to Christ for someone you know?
